sentences.text: Arguments on the maintainability of the present appeal were heard.
The appeal file and the case file are carefully perused.
4. Ld.
Counsel for the respondents questioned the maintainability of the appeal.
He argued that no appeal can be filed before this court on the ground that the sentence awarded by the Ld. Trial Court was inadequate.
He mentioned that filing of appeal is a statutory remedy and the same cannot be availed unless specifically provided under the Code of Criminal Procedure.

He contended that the appeal for enhancement of sentence could have been filed strictly in accordance with Section 377 CrPC and the said provision does not give any right of appeal to the appellant before this court.

In order to support these submissions, he placed reliance on the decision in the matter of Bhajanpura Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Limited Vs. Sushil Kumar in Crl. Appeal No.972/2012 decided by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi on 03.09.2014.
5.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: On the other hand, Ld. Counsel for the appellant contended that this appeal is legally maintainable.
He submitted that the appeal has been filed not only for enhancement of sentence but also on the ground of inadequacy of compensation.
He mentioned that the appeal on the ground of inadequacy of compensation is maintainable before this court.
He contended that the Ld. Trial Court has taken an exceptionally lenient view by sentencing the respondents with fine only.
He argued that Ld. Trial Court failed to take note of the fact that respondents were habitual offenders and they defrauded various other persons.
He mentioned that the Ld. Trial Court failed to appreciate that respondents did not deserve a lenient view.

He contended that maximum substantive sentence provided for the offence punishable under Section 138 NI Act is two years'
imprisonment.
However, no substantive sentence has been awarded to respondent no.2.
He contended that the sentence and the compensation are inadequate and the same should be enhanced.

In order to support these submissions, he has placed reliance on the decision in the matter of Sugarthi Suresh Kumar Vs. Jagdishan 2002 (2) SCC 420.
6.

entities.text: Sugarthi Suresh Kumar Vs. Jagdishan 2002 (2) SCC 420
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In terms of the present appeal, the appellant has sought enhancement of the substantive sentence and compensation on the ground that the Ld. Trial Court has taken an exceptionally lenient view.
It has been argued on behalf of the appellant that the Ld. Trial Court failed to take note of the fact that respondents were habitual offenders.
The appeal contains a prayer that the order on sentence may be modified and a strict substantive sentence should be awarded apart from enhancing the compensation.
On the other hand, respondents have questioned the maintainability of this appeal.
7. In order to deal with this argument, it would be necessary to refer the relevant provisions of appeal under the Code of Criminal Procedure.

Section 372 of CrPC provides that no appeal shall lie unless otherwise provided and it reads as under:

2 "372.

sentences.text: No appeal to lie unless otherwise provided - No appeal shall lie from any judgment or order of a Criminal Court except as provided for by this Code or by any other law for the time being in force.

[Provided that the victim shall have a right to prefer an appeal against any order passed by the Court acquitting the accused or convicting for a lesser offence or imposing inadequate compensation, and such appeal shall lie to the Court to which an appeal ordinarily lies against the order of conviction of such Court.]
[Inserted by the Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2008 (5 of 2009), Section 29.]"

entities.text: Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2008 (5 of 2009), Section 29
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: 8. Thus, as per Section 372 CrPC, no appeal would lie from any judgment or an order of a criminal court except as provided for by the Code of Criminal Procedure or any other law.

The proviso to Section 372 CrPC provides that a victim shall have a right to file an appeal against the order of the court acquitting the accused or convicting him for a lesser offence or imposing inadequate compensation and such appeal shall lie to the court to which an appeal shall ordinarily lie against conviction.
This proviso was inserted by means of an amendment made vide Act 5 of 2009 which came into effect from 31.12.2009.

The proviso created a right for the victim to file an appeal in respect of situations mentioned therein but the complainant in the proceedings under Section 138 NI Act cannot be equated or treated at par with the 'victim' for whose benefit the amendment was brought into existence.
It was meant only for those victims, on whose behalf primarily, State used to prosecute the offenders.
The amendment gave a voice to the victim to challenge the acquittal by filing an appeal under Section 372 CrPC.
It was a right conferred upon the victim to prefer an appeal on limited grounds.
It is separate and independent statutory right which is not dependent or subservient to the right of appeal of the State but no such right was conferred on the complainant.
9. Therefore, the appellant being complainant of the proceedings under Section 138 NI Act cannot be termed as 'victim' under the proviso of Section 372 CrPC.

The said view finds strength from the judgment of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Bhajanpura Cooperative Urban Thrift & Credit Society Limited (supra) and its relevant portion is reproduced as under:-
"13.

sentences.text: In my considered view, the 'complainant' in the proceedings under Section 138 N.I.Act cannot be considered 'victim' in the letter and spirit of the definition of Section 2 (wa) of the Code and definition of 'injury' under Section 44 IPC cannot be imported into Section 138 N.I.Act.
In every such proceedings at first instance, every complainant considers/claims himself/herself a 'victim'.

The complainants in these proceedings cannot be taken at par with those who put criminal law into motion to bring the offenders to book at whose hands, they have sustained 'injury' as defined in Section 44 IPC.
The changes in Cr.P.C. were for 'victims' who were the worst sufferers in a crime and did not have much role in the Court proceedings.
To avoid distortion of the Criminal Judicial System, they were given certain rights.
14. The controversy now is no longer res integra in view of the pronouncement of law by Supreme Court in 'Subhash Chand vs. State (Delhi Administration)', (2013) 2 SCC 17.

sentences.text:
The State filed criminal appeal before the Sessions Court under Section 378 (1)(a) Cr.P.C.
Preliminary objection regarding maintainability of the appeal before the Sessions Court was rejected.
That order was challenged before this Court (Delhi High Court) and it was held that Sessions Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal.

The order of the High Court was challenged before the Supreme Court who remanded the case to this Court for fresh decision after taking into consideration the provisions of Sections 378(1) and 378(4) of Cr.P.C. and the relevant provisions of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.

After remand, this Court held that the appeal filed by the State against an order of acquittal would lie to the Sessions Court under Section 378 (1)
of the Cr.P.C.

Again, this order was challenged by the accused before the Supreme Court and Supreme Court held:
"....we conclude that a complainant can file an application for special leave to appeal against an order of acquittal of any kind only to the High Court.
He cannot file such appeal in the Sessions Court.
The complainant can challenge the order of acquittal by filing an application for special leave to appeal in the Delhi High Court and not in the Sessions Court...."
(Emphasis supplied).
10. Accordingly, the appellant cannot take the benefit of the proviso to Section 372 CrPC for filing of appeal.
Even otherwise, the said right has been given to the victim against the acquittal of the accused or convicting for lesser offence or imposing inadequate compensation.
Therefore, the said right of appeal to the victim is not available for inadequacy of substantive sentence.

Hence, even if the appellant would have been treated at par with 'victim' of proviso to Section 372 CrPC, he could not have invoked the said provision for filing of the present appeal for inadequacy of substantive sentence.
11. It is well settled jurisprudence that the remedy of appeal is creature of the Statute.
Unless same is provided either under Code of Criminal Procedure or by any other law for the time being in force no appeal is maintainable.
Therefore, in the succeeding paragraphs, it is proposed to be discussed if any provision of law permits filing of this appeal.
12. In the present appeal, the appellant has sought two reliefs i.e. (i) enhancement of substantive sentence of respondents and (ii) enhancement of the compensation amount.

The appeal for enhancement of sentence can only be filed under Section 377 CrPC which provides as under:
"377. Appeal by the State Government against sentence - (1) Save as otherwise provided in sub-section (2), the State Government may, in any case of conviction on a trial held by any Court other than a High Court, direct the Public Prosecutor to present [an appeal against the sentence on the ground of its inadequacy- Mr Sachin Assal vs Ms Sampatti Trading And Developers Ltd on 22 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/54558959/
4 (a) to the Court of Session, if the sentence is passed by the Magistrate; and (b) to the High Court, if the sentence is passed by any other Court.]

(2) If such conviction is in a case in which the offence has been investigated by the Delhi Special Police Establishment, constituted under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act,
1946 (25 of 1946), or by any other agency empowered to make investigation into an offence under any Central Act other than this Code, [the Central Government may also direct] [Substituted by Act 45 of 1978, Section 29, for "the Central Government may direct", w.e.f. 18.12.1978.] the Public Prosecutor to present [ an appeal against the sentence on the ground of its inadequacy- (a) to the Court of Session, if the sentence is passed by the Magistrate; and (b) to the High Court, if the sentence is passed by any other Court.]

sentences.text: (3)When an appeal has been filed against the sentence on the ground of its inadequacy,[the Court of Session or, as the case may be the High Court] [Substituted by the Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2005 (25 of 2005), Section 31 (b), for "the High Court" (w.e.f. 23-6-2006).] shall not enhance the sentence except after giving to the accused a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against such enhancement and while showing cause, the accused may plead for his acquittal or for the reduction of the sentence.

(4) [When an appeal has been filed against a sentence passed under section 376, section 376A, section 376AB, section 376B, section 376C,
section 376D, section 376DA, section 376DB or section 376E of the Indian Penal Code, the appeal shall be disposed of within a period of six months from the date of filing of such appeal.]
[Inserted by Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2018 (22 of 2018), dated 11.8.2018.]."
13. The aforesaid provision expressly provides that it is the State Government which has the power to direct the filing of appeal for enhancement of sentence and none else.
The said provision applies not only to the state cases but also to any trial conducted for any type of case.

entities.text: Praveen Kansal Vs. State 2020 SCC OnLine SC 684
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: While the victim is given opportunity to prefer appeal in the event of imposing inadequate compensation, but at the same time there is no provision for appeal by the victim for questioning the order of sentence as inadequate, whereas Section 377 Cr.P.C gives the power to the State Government to prefer appeal for enhancement of sentence.

While it is open for the State Government to prefer appeal for inadequate sentence under Section 377 Cr.P.C but similarly no appeal can be maintained by victim under Section 372 Cr.P.C on the ground of inadequate Mr Sachin Assal vs Ms Sampatti Trading And Developers Ltd on 22 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/54558959/
5 sentence.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is fairly well settled that the remedy of appeal is creature of the Statute.

Unless same is provided either under Code of Criminal Procedure or by any other law for the time being in force no appeal, seeking enhancement of sentence at the instance of the victim is maintainable."

14. Therefore, in absence of any statutory provision in that regard, the present appeal of the complainant for the offence punishable under Section 138 NI Act for seeking enhancement of substantive sentence of the respondents is not maintainable.

15. Now, turning to the second relief claimed by the appellant in respect of inadequacy of compensation, record shows that the Ld. Trial Court sentenced the respondents to fine of Rs.1,23,428/- and directed that the same shall be disbursed to the appellant as compensation.
( 4) An order under this section may also be made by an Appellate Court or by the High Court or Court of sessions when exercising its power of revision.

(5) At the time of awarding compensation in any subsequent civil suit relating to the same matter,
the court shall take into account any sum paid or recovered as compensation under this section."
16.
Thus, as per the said provision, the compensation can be awarded only where fine does not form the part of sentence.

It has been held in the matter of State of Punjab Vs. Gurmeet Singh 2002 (6)
SCC 663 that a reading of Sub-Section (3) of Section 357 CrPC shows that the question of award of compensation would arise where the court imposes a sentence of which fine does not form a part.

entities.text:
State of Punjab Vs. Gurmeet Singh 2002 (6)
SCC 663
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Further, it was held in the matter of Sivasuriyan Vs. Thangavelu 2004 (13) SCC 975 that apart from Section 357(3) CrPC, there is no other provision under the Code where the court can direct payment of compensation.

It was observed in this matter that power under Section 357(3) CrPC can be Mr Sachin Assal vs Ms Sampatti Trading And Developers Ltd on 22 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/54558959/
6 exercised only when the court imposes sentence of which fine does not form a part.

entities.text: Mr Sachin Assal vs Ms Sampatti Trading And Developers Ltd
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 17. Thus, it is evident from Section 357(3) CrPC that where the sentence imposed does not include a fine, it can direct the accused to pay, by way of compensation, such amount as may be specified in the order to the person who suffered any loss or injury.

However, Sub- Section (1) of Section 357 CrPC provides that where the court imposes a sentence of fine or a sentence of which fine forms a part, the court may direct the fine amount to be applied in the payment to any person as compensation for loss or injury when in the opinion of the court, the compensation is recoverable by such person in a civil court.
If compensation could be paid out of fine, there is no need to award separate compensation.

Reliance in this regard can be placed on the decision by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the matter of R.Vijayan Vs. Baby & Anr. 2012 (1) SCC 260 wherein it is observed as follows:
"18.

Having reached that stage, if some Magistrates go by the traditional view that the criminal proceedings are for imposing punishment on the accused, either imprisonment or fine or both, and there is no need to compensate the complainant, particularly if the complainant is not a 'victim' in the real sense, but is a well-to-do financier or financing institution, difficulties and complications arise.

In those cases where the discretion to direct payment of compensation is not exercised, it causes considerable difficulty to the complainant, as invariably, by the time the criminal case is decided, the limitation for filing civil cases would have expired.

As the provisions of Chapter XVII of the Act strongly lean towards grant of reimbursement of the loss by way of compensation, the courts should, unless there are special circumstances, in all cases of conviction, uniformly exercise the power to levy fine upto twice the cheque amount (keeping in view the cheque amount and the simple interest thereon at 9% per annum as the reasonable quantum of loss) and direct payment of such amount as compensation.

Direction to pay compensation by way of restitution in regard to the loss on account of dishonour of the cheque should be practical and realistic, which would mean not only the payment of the cheque amount but interest thereon at a reasonable rate.
Uniformity and consistency in deciding similar cases by different courts, not only increase the credibility of cheque as a negotiable instrument, but also the credibility of courts of justice."
18. The question of awarding compensation under Section 357(3) CrPC arise only in those cases where the court has not imposed any fine on the accused.
In the present matter, the Ld. Trial Court imposed maximum legally permissible fine of double the amount of cheque and directed that the same shall be disbursed to the appellant as compensation.

No doubt, the Ld. Trial Court wrongly mentioned in the impugned order on sentence that the compensation should be disbursed under Section 357(3) CrPC rather than Section 357(1)(b) CrPC but it does not alter the factual situation that it imposed a fine of double the amount of cheque on the respondents and directed that the same shall be disbursed to the appellant as compensation.
In view of this, the argument that the appeal is maintainable on the ground of inadequacy of compensation is misconceived.
19. In view of the above discussion and taking into account the unequivocal interpretation of Hon'ble Higher Courts of the appeal provisions, this appeal is not maintainable.
Accordingly, the present appeal is dismissed.
